Grain Silos Go Electric

By Tobias Renn

Cooperatives across the invented Halvard County are replacing propane grain dryers with electric heat pumps, a change their managers say has cut drying costs by a quarter since the first units were installed two harvests ago.

The switch was paid for in part by a county grant that covers forty percent of the equipment cost for any cooperative that also installs rooftop solar on its storage buildings. Eleven of the county's fourteen cooperatives have applied.

Managers said the heat pumps dry grain more slowly than propane burners, which means harvest crews have had to adjust schedules. In wet years, some cooperatives keep a propane dryer as a backup for the busiest weeks.

Utility planners expect the new load to peak in October, when most grain is dried, and say the county's grid can carry it without new transmission lines for at least the next five years.
